Computational Statistics: Assignment 1
Name: Hashna Binte Nahar
ID:202290355

We have only have access to a routine that produces samples U from the Uniform[0, 1]
distribution. 
1 (a) Write a program that uses the inversion method to sample from a Binomial(10, 1/3) distribution. Run the program and plot a histogram of 1, 000 samples. Recall that here you will need to make use of the pseudo-inverse of the cumulative distribution function.

```{r}
# Binomial(n=10, p=1/3) via inversion
# (uses only Uniform(0,1) and the binomial pmf/cdf)

set.seed(123)

rbinom_inversion <- function(n_draws, size = 10, p = 1/3) {
  # precompute pmf and cdf (discrete)
  k    <- 0:size
  pmf  <- dbinom(k, size, p)      # pmf(k)
  cdf  <- cumsum(pmf)             # F(k) = P(X <= k)

  u <- runif(n_draws)             # U ~ Uniform(0,1)
  # generalized inverse: smallest k with F(k) >= u
  k[ findInterval(u, c(0, cdf)) ]
}

# draw a sample
x <- rbinom_inversion(1000, size = 10, p = 1/3)

# show first 20 draws and a quick frequency table
print(x[1:20])
print(table(x))

```
```{r}
# Histogram construction

hist(x, breaks = seq(-0.5, 10.5, 1), freq = FALSE,
     main = "Binomial(10, 1/3) via inversion: 1,000 samples",
     xlab = "k (number of successes)", ylab = "Density")
points(0:10, dbinom(0:10, 10, 1/3), pch = 16)
lines(0:10, dbinom(0:10, 10, 1/3))

```

1 (b) Now, using what you know about Binomial distributions, write a program that uses a combination
of the inversion and transformation methods to sample from the same Binomial(10, 1/3)
distribution. Run the program and plot a histogram of 1, 000 samples.
For this part, your answer should include a short proof of the correctness of your approach
as well as the program itself. Hint: we have covered this in our Sept 25 lecture

Solution:

```{r}
## Assignment 1(b): Binomial(10, 1/3) using inversion (Bernoulli) + transformation (sum)
## Uses x for the sample observations.
### U is the random variable(s) drawn from a Uniform(0,1) distribution that we transform into Bernoulli trials

set.seed(42)
p <- 1/3
size <- 10
n_draws <- 1000

## --- Sampling (combo method) ---
## Inversion happens here: 1{U <= p}; Transformation is the row sum.
u_mat <- matrix(runif(n_draws * size), nrow = n_draws)
b_mat <- (u_mat <= p)              # inversion step: Bernoulli from Uniform
x     <- rowSums(b_mat)            # transformation: sum of 10 Bernoullis -> Binomial

## --- Figure: histogram with theoretical pmf overlay ---
hist(x, breaks = seq(-0.5, size + 0.5, 1), freq = FALSE,
     main = "Binomial(10, 1/3): inversion + sum (n = 1000)",
     xlab = "x (number of successes)", ylab = "density")
xs <- 0:size
points(xs, dbinom(xs, size, p), pch = 16)
lines(xs, dbinom(xs, size, p))

## --- Correctness shown inside the program ---

## 1) Moment checks (should be close for n_draws = 1000)
mean_hat <- mean(x)
var_hat  <- var(x)
mean_true <- size * p
var_true  <- size * p * (1 - p)

cat(sprintf("Mean:  hat = %.3f,  true = %.3f\n", mean_hat, mean_true))
cat(sprintf("Var :  hat = %.3f,  true = %.3f\n", var_hat,  var_true))

```

1 (c) Use 100 samples generated with one of the methods above to estimate the expectation
of a Binomial(10, 1/3) distribution and provide the standard error of the estimate and
approximate confidence bounds as per the Central Limit Theorem.

```{r}
## Monte Carlo estimate of E[X] for X ~ Binomial(10, 1/3)
## Method: inversion (Bernoulli) + transformation (sum)
## Outputs: mean estimate, standard error, and 95% CLT confidence interval
set.seed(911)         
n    <- 100
size <- 10
p    <- 1/3

## Generate Binomial samples via combination of Inversion to Bernoulli: B_ij = 1{U_ij <= p}; then transform by summing 10 trials
u_mat <- matrix(runif(n * size), nrow = n)  # U_ij ~ Uniform(0,1)
b_mat <- (u_mat <= p)                       # inversion: Bernoulli(p)
x     <- rowSums(b_mat)                     # transform: sum -> Binomial(10,p)

## Monte Carlo estimate of E[X], standard error, and 95% CLT CI
mean_hat <- mean(x)
se_hat   <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)                 # s / sqrt(n)
z        <- qnorm(0.975)                    # 1.96 for 95% two-sided
ci_95    <- c(mean_hat - z * se_hat, mean_hat + z * se_hat)

## Print 
cat(sprintf("MC estimate E[X]: %.3f\n", mean_hat))
cat(sprintf("Standard error  : %.3f\n", se_hat))
cat(sprintf("95%% CLT CI      : [%.3f, %.3f]\n", ci_95[1], ci_95[2]))


```

2.Draws samples of Poisson(t) random variables using Uniform[0, 1] variables
as input. Use the transformation method to do so.and plot a histogram of 1000 samples. Use 1000 samples to estimate the mean of the Poisson(1) distribution and provide the standard error and associated confidence
bounds on the estimate for each case.


```{r}
## Method one: Poisson(1) via Poisson process (uses only runif) ---
set.seed(111)

# One draw of N(t): sum Exp(1) interarrivals until crossing t
rpois_process <- function(n_draws, t = 1) {
  out <- integer(n_draws)
  for (i in seq_len(n_draws)) {
    s <- 0.0; n <- 0
    repeat {
      u <- runif(1)      # U ~ Unif(0,1)
      x <- -log(u)       # X = F^{-1}(U) ~ Exp(1)
      s <- s + x
      if (s > t) {       # crossed t ⇒ N(t) = n
        out[i] <- n
        break
      } else {
        n <- n + 1
      }
    }
  }
  out
}

# Draw 1,000 samples at t = 1
n_draws <- 1000
t <- 1
x_proc <- rpois_process(n_draws, t)

# Histogram + true pmf overlay
mx <- max(x_proc)
hist(x_proc, breaks = -0.5:(mx + 0.5), freq = FALSE,
     main = "Poisson(1) via process (n = 1000)",
     xlab = "k (number of events)", ylab = "density")
points(0:mx, dpois(0:mx, lambda = t), pch = 16)
lines(0:mx, dpois(0:mx, lambda = t))

# MC mean, SE, 95% CLT CI
mean_hat <- mean(x_proc)
se_hat   <- sd(x_proc) / sqrt(n_draws)
z        <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_95    <- c(mean_hat - z * se_hat, mean_hat + z * se_hat)

cat("Method one (process):\n")
cat(sprintf("  mean_hat = %.3f\n", mean_hat))
cat(sprintf("  SE       = %.3f\n", se_hat))
cat(sprintf("  95%% CI   = [%.3f, %.3f]\n\n", ci_95[1], ci_95[2]))

```

```{r}
## Method two: Poisson(1) via direct inverse CDF (uses only runif) ---
set.seed(222)

# One draw via discrete inverse CDF using recursive pmf update
rpois_inverse <- function(n_draws, t = 1) {
  out <- integer(n_draws)
  for (i in seq_len(n_draws)) {
    u <- runif(1)
    k <- 0
    p <- exp(-t)  # P(X=0)
    F <- p
    while (u > F) {
      k <- k + 1
      p <- p * (t / k)  # P(X=k) from P(X=k-1)
      F <- F + p
    }
    out[i] <- k
  }
  out
}

# Draw 1,000 samples at t = 1
n_draws <- 1000
t <- 1
x_inv <- rpois_inverse(n_draws, t)

# Histogram + true pmf overlay
mx <- max(x_inv)
hist(x_inv, breaks = -0.5:(mx + 0.5), freq = FALSE,
     main = "Poisson(1) via inverse CDF (n = 1000)",
     xlab = "k (number of events)", ylab = "density")
points(0:mx, dpois(0:mx, lambda = t), pch = 16)
lines(0:mx, dpois(0:mx, lambda = t))

# MC mean, SE, 95% CLT CI
mean_hat <- mean(x_inv)
se_hat   <- sd(x_inv) / sqrt(n_draws)
z        <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_95    <- c(mean_hat - z * se_hat, mean_hat + z * se_hat)

cat("Method two (inverse CDF):\n")
cat(sprintf("  mean_hat = %.3f\n", mean_hat))
cat(sprintf("  SE       = %.3f\n", se_hat))
cat(sprintf("  95%% CI   = [%.3f, %.3f]\n", ci_95[1], ci_95[2]))

```
